findings.title: call_llm never records usage — real spend leaves no row in api_usage_logs

locations: server/llm.py:369 (call_llm — no accounting anywhere in its body)
callers with no metering context: server/agent_session.py:178, server/draft.py:142, server/humanizer.py:589, server/humanize_skill.py:520, server/assignment_dump.py:128
evidence.repro: grep -nE 'log_api_call|record_service_cost|meter_user|api_usage' server/llm.py  -> zero matches inside call_llm. Then run a production path (study-material generation) against a scratch DB and count ApiUsageLog rows.
evidence.observed: ApiUsageLog rows recorded: 0, while the user was charged 1 token against a true measured cost of 500 tokens ($0.05). Reproduced by agy scratch repro_econ01.py; the absence of any accounting call in call_llm re-confirmed by reading llm.py:369-560 at HEAD.

findings.impact: Every non-streaming LLM call is billed to the user and invisible to the ledger. Cost analytics, the monitors cost panel, margin reporting and the credit engine's measured pricing all under-report. This is the same class that was fixed for stream_llm in commit 7662373 and call_llm was missed.

fix.approach: Record usage inside call_llm itself via the existing server/metering.py contextvar rather than adding a db parameter to every caller. record_service_cost() is already fail-soft when no user is in context, and stream_llm already proves the mechanism.

findings.title: _charge_tokens deducts the balance and writes NO CreditTransaction row
findings.correction: The report blamed server/credits.py charge(). That is WRONG: charge() writes the ledger row at credits.py:404-408. The live defect is _charge_tokens in routes_overlord.py — the hand-rolled debit the agent paths actually call.

locations: server/credits.py:404-408 (charge(), which does it correctly — contrast)
evidence.repro: python3 -c """from server.database import User, CreditTransaction; from server.routes_overlord import _charge_tokens; u=User(public_id='t',settings={'token_balance':10000.0}); ... count rows before/after"""
evidence.observed: balance 10000.0 -> 9900.0 (100 deducted) while the CreditTransaction row count is UNCHANGED. Body read at HEAD: `settings['token_balance']=max(0.0,bal-cost); user.settings=settings; db.commit()` — no ledger write, and no with_for_update.

findings.impact: Every agent action is charged with no ledger record. No audit trail, refunds cannot be computed, and the balance can silently diverge from the sum of CreditTransaction deltas, so any reconciliation from the ledger disagrees with reality.

fix.approach: Delegate to credits.charge, which already writes the ledger row AND takes the row lock. _charge_tokens predates the ledger and duplicates it worse.

snippets.before:
def _charge_tokens(user, db, cost: float) -> None:
    """Deduct from the user's token budget (settings.token_balance) after work ran.
    Credits are untouched (they are the discount currency)."""
    settings = dict(user.settings or {})
    bal = float(settings.get("token_balance", 0) or 0)
    settings["token_balance"] = max(0.0, bal - cost)
    user.settings = settings
    db.commit()
snippets.after:
def _charge_tokens(user, db, cost: float) -> None:
    """Deduct from the user's token budget after work ran.

    Delegates to credits.charge so the debit also lands in the ledger and takes the
    row lock. The previous hand-rolled body moved the JSON balance and committed
    while writing NO CreditTransaction row, so agent spend was invisible to every
    audit and refund path.
    """
    from .credits import charge
    charge(user, "agent_action", db, cost_override=cost, reason="agent_action")

fix.risk: charge() returns False on insufficient balance instead of clamping to 0 — a behaviour change from silent overdraft-to-zero to a refused charge. Correct semantics, but the agent loop's expectation must be checked.

findings.title: Rate limiting keys on request.client.host, always 127.0.0.1 behind the tunnel — one shared bucket for all users

locations: server/main.py:300-310 (another path that DOES read x-forwarded-for — the app knows the header exists)
evidence.repro: grep -n 'client_ip' server/ratelimit.py; then hit a rate-limited route max_requests+1 times and observe that a second, unrelated client also receives 429.
evidence.observed: Read at HEAD: `client_ip = request.client.host if request.client else "unknown"` -> `key = f"{client_ip}:{request.url.path}"`. cloudflared is the only ingress (helpotron.dpdns.org -> 127.0.0.1:5000), so this is 127.0.0.1 for every user on earth. The bucket is per-path, globally.

findings.impact: Two failures at once: no abuser is ever limited for their own traffic, and any single client can deny a route to every user by burning the shared bucket. Affects signup, login, recovery and help-ticket routes alike.

dependents: every route decorated with the rate_limit dependency

fix.approach: Resolve client identity from the forwarding header, but ONLY when the immediate peer is the trusted proxy. Taken unconditionally the header is attacker-controlled and would give every request its own bucket and no limit at all — so the trust check is the whole point, not a detail.

snippets.after:
# The tunnel is the only ingress, so the socket peer is always 127.0.0.1 and a
# per-socket key collapses every user onto one bucket. Trust the forwarding header
# ONLY from that hop — honoured unconditionally it is attacker-controlled, and a
# spoofed value would give every request its own bucket and no limit at all.
TRUSTED_PROXY_HOSTS = {"127.0.0.1", "::1"}


def client_identity(request: Request) -> str:
    peer = request.client.host if request.client else "unknown"
    if peer in TRUSTED_PROXY_HOSTS:
        fwd = request.headers.get("cf-connecting-ip") or request.headers.get("x-forwarded-for", "")
        first = fwd.split(",")[0].strip()
        if first:
            return first
    return peer


RATE_LIMITS: dict[str, list[float]] = defaultdict(list)

fix.migration: RATE_LIMITS has no eviction and grows unbounded — add a sweep of stale keys while here.
fix.risk: If uvicorn is ever exposed directly, TRUSTED_PROXY_HOSTS must not include public peers. It is 127.0.0.1/::1 only, correct for this box.

tests.name: test_rate_limit_separates_clients_behind_the_proxy
tests.proves: two forwarded clients get independent buckets, and an untrusted peer cannot spoof one
tests.body:
def test_rate_limit_separates_clients_behind_the_proxy():
    from server.ratelimit import client_identity

    class _Req:
        def __init__(self, peer, headers):
            self.client = type("C", (), {"host": peer})()
            self.headers = headers

    a = client_identity(_Req("127.0.0.1", {"cf-connecting-ip": "203.0.113.7"}))
    b = client_identity(_Req("127.0.0.1", {"cf-connecting-ip": "203.0.113.8"}))
    assert a != b, "every user collapses onto one rate-limit bucket"

    spoof = client_identity(_Req("198.51.100.9", {"x-forwarded-for": "1.2.3.4"}))
    assert spoof == "198.51.100.9", "a spoofed header from an untrusted peer was honoured"

findings.title: Read-modify-write on the User.settings JSON blob with no row lock — concurrent writes silently discard one another

locations: server/credits.py:391 (charge() — the correct pattern, for contrast)
evidence.repro: Two sessions on one row: read settings in both, write a different key in each, commit both. The second commit overwrites the first's key.
evidence.observed: Read at HEAD. `settings` is a JSON blob, so no single UPDATE can express the merge atomically; the only available protection is SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the row. charge() takes it (credits.py:391); these two do not.

findings.impact: Two concurrent requests lose one another's settings. The financial case is the serious one: two concurrent agent charges each read the same balance and both debit it, overdrawing the account while both responses report success. AGENTS.md already records this class and the rule that money paths must lock.

fix.approach: Take the row lock for the read-modify-write, exactly as charge() does. ECON-03's fix to _charge_tokens removes the second unlocked site by delegating to charge().

snippets.after:
# Locked for the read-modify-write: `settings` is a JSON blob, so this cannot
        # be a single atomic UPDATE, and two concurrent writers would otherwise each
        # read the same dict and the second would silently discard the first's key.
        locked = db.query(User).filter(User.id == user.id).with_for_update().first()
        if locked is not None:
            user = locked
        current = UserSettingsService.get_user_settings(user)

fix.risk: A writer that raises inside the lock must rollback or it holds the row until the request session closes — the hazard credits.py already documents.

findings.title: usage_percent reads the DEAD discount column, so it returns 100% for every user permanently and Telegram fires a false alert

locations: server/payments.py:351-357 (a second, stale plan_limits table predating the 100x token unit)
evidence.repro: python3: u=User(plan='pro', credits=0.0, settings={'token_balance':100000.0}); print(get_token_balance(u), usage_percent(u))
evidence.observed: REAL balance 100000.0 -> usage_percent 100.0 -> telegram fires >=80 True. After using 70k of 100k -> still 100.0. The function is structurally incapable of returning anything but 100, because it reads `user.credits` (the earn-only discount field, 0.0 for every normal user) instead of settings['token_balance']. Confirmed by direct execution at HEAD.

findings.impact: Every user on the alert sweep receives a false 'you have used 100% of your credits' warning regardless of balance, and the number never moves as tokens are actually spent — so the alert cannot detect a real exhaustion either. It is both a false positive and a blind spot.

fix.approach: Read the real balance and derive the percentage from it. The plan allowances are already canonical in credits.TIER_MONTHLY_CREDITS — the local plan_limits dict is a stale second copy from before the 100x unit change, so replace it rather than editing it.

snippets.after:
def usage_percent(user: User) -> float:
    """Percentage of the plan's monthly TOKEN allowance consumed.

    This read `user.credits` — the earn-only discount column, 0.0 for every normal
    user — so `used = limit - 0` and it returned 100.0 for everybody, permanently,
    while the real balance sat unread in settings['token_balance']. The alert that
    consumes it (telegram_bot.py:182) therefore warned every user they were
    exhausted and could never detect an actual exhaustion.
    """
    from .credits import get_token_balance, TIER_MONTHLY_CREDITS

    plan = getattr(user, "plan", None) or "trial"
    limit = float(TIER_MONTHLY_CREDITS.get(plan, 0) or 0)
    if limit <= 0:
        return 0.0
    remaining = float(get_token_balance(user) or 0.0)
    used = max(0.0, limit - remaining)
    return min(100.0, (used / limit) * 100.0)

fix.risk: TIER_MONTHLY_CREDITS is imported lazily inside the function to avoid an import cycle — credits imports payments at module scope, so the reverse must be deferred.

def test_usage_percent_reads_the_real_token_balance():

    from server.payments import usage_percent

findings.title: Resource guard has no absolute memory floor and fails open silently — the cap does not exist in the window it was built for
findings.correction: The report said 'fails open under concurrent burst, no swap gating'. At HEAD the fail-open is on an UNREADABLE METRIC, not on concurrency, and it is documented as deliberate. Reframed rather than dropped: the consequence is still real on a box that has twice been taken into swap death.

locations: server/resource_guard.py:22-24 (the swap rationale in the docstring)
evidence.repro: Read at HEAD: `if st['ram_pct'] is None and st['cpu_pct'] is None: return True` with the comment 'failing open keeps the product usable'.
evidence.observed: No swap or absolute-memory metric participates in the admission decision at all. The module docstring records that a swap-pinned box caused this twice on this machine, yet swap is not among the gates.

findings.impact: On a metric source that behaves differently, or during the first-caller window before prime_cpu_sample warms, the cap silently does not apply and the queue does not engage — precisely when the box is at risk. The trigger is an unreadable metric, not concurrency.

dependents: the two heaviest agent paths that call admit()

fix.approach: Keep fail-open for a genuinely unknown platform, but narrow it and make it visible on Linux, and add MemAvailable as an absolute floor so a swap-pinned box is caught even when the percentage reads as tolerable.

snippets.anchor:
if st["ram_pct"] is None and st["cpu_pct"] is None:
        return True
snippets.before:
if st["ram_pct"] is None and st["cpu_pct"] is None:
        return True
snippets.after:
if st["ram_pct"] is None and st["cpu_pct"] is None:
        # Failing open keeps the product usable where /proc differs. On Linux an
        # unreadable metric means the cap silently does not exist on the one box it
        # was written for, so say so instead of hiding it.
        if sys.platform.startswith("linux"):
            logger.warning(
                "resource guard: metrics unreadable on Linux — admission control is "
                "INACTIVE for this call"
            )
        return True

    # An absolute floor catches a swap-pinned box that the percentage alone reads as
    # tolerable. MemAvailable is the honest figure, not free's 'free' column.
    floor = float(os.environ.get("RESOURCE_GUARD_MIN_AVAILABLE_MB", MIN_AVAILABLE_MB))
    if st.get("mem_available_mb") is not None and st["mem_available_mb"] < floor:
        return False

fix.migration: Add MIN_AVAILABLE_MB = 3000.0 (the measured safe level for this machine) and surface mem_available_mb in budget_status(); make it env-overridable so it tunes without a code change.
fix.risk: A hard floor can refuse work on a healthy-but-busy box. 3000 MB is the documented budget here; the env override exists for that.

findings.title: REFUTED — the 10,000x token miscalculation is in DEAD CODE and cannot reach a user
findings.original_claim: payments.process_payment grants 1 token per dollar instead of 10,000, so a $10 payment yields 10 tokens.
findings.correction: The arithmetic is real — payments.py:284 computes `amount_cents / 100.0`, which is 1 token per dollar against TOKENS_PER_USD = 10_000 (credits.py:58) — but the value can never reach a user. payments.py:308 hardcodes `status = "pending"`, and the return at :335-337 gates on `if status == "captured"`, so tokens_added is always reported as 0. Line 319 states it outright: 'No grant lives here any more, deliberately.' That was the SEC-2026-001 fix: a caller naming provider='stripe' used to mint tokens with no processor involved.
findings.verified_by: Read server/payments.py:296-341 at HEAD. The live grant path is handle_stripe_webhook (payments.py:201, :229), which reads TIER_TOKENS — the canonical allowance table — and is granted only on a signed checkout.session.completed.
findings.residual_risk: Real but low: the stale `tokens_added` expression and the stale `plan_limits` copy elsewhere are traps for the next reader, and a future edit that re-enables granting here would silently under-pay by 10,000x. The `tokens_added` variable should be deleted rather than left as a plausible-looking constant.
findings.action: Delete the dead `tokens_added` computation and its two return keys, replacing them with an explicit 0 and a comment naming handle_stripe_webhook as the grant path. No behavioural change; removes the trap.
findings.test: No test added — the assertion would pin dead code. Instead assert the live path: posting /api/checkout must NOT change token_balance.

findings.title: REFUTED — GDPR deletion is NOT inert; it is a real transactional hard delete
findings.original_claim: 'GDPR permanent delete is 100% inert — no worker ever reads the pending_deletion key.'
findings.correction: There is no `pending_deletion` key anywhere in the codebase. A full-repo grep across *.py, *.js and *.jsx returns ZERO matches, so there is no key for a worker to fail to read. The real implementation is an immediate synchronous erasure.
findings.verified_by: grep -rn pending_deletion --include=*.py --include=*.js --include=*.jsx . -> no matches. Then read server/privacy.py:62-95: delete_user_account_and_data iterates _CHILD_TABLES issuing per-table deletes (with special handling for Referral, SharedMaterial, StudyGroup), deletes the User row, and commits once — documented as 'Runs as one transaction — if any step fails the whole erasure rolls back'.
findings.residual_risk: Genuinely worth checking, and the report's instinct was not worthless: the erasure covers the TABLES in _CHILD_TABLES. Whether that list is COMPLETE against the current models is the real question — an omission would leave orphaned personal data while returning success. That is a legitimate follow-up, not the finding that was filed.
findings.action: Replace with a coverage test: assert every model carrying a user_id FK is either in _CHILD_TABLES or explicitly exempted. That catches a future model being added without erasure coverage.

findings.title: REFUTED — the blocking hygiene call was already fixed; the report described the pre-fix state

findings.correction: Already remediated. server/routes_hygiene.py:54 wraps the call in `await asyncio.to_thread(lambda: httpx.post(...))`, with a comment recording the original defect ('It blocked the whole event loop, so ONE request...'). findings.title: Elite plan bypasses BOTH the token gate and the charge on dump finalization — unlimited free expensive work
findings.correction: The report claimed '~12 routes'. There is no such broad exemption — is_unmetered() is correctly operator-only and the other sites use it. There is exactly ONE real site, and the report understated it: it is two conditions, not one, so the gate AND the charge both skip Elite.

locations: server/routes_dump.py:422 (the PRE-FLIGHT gate: `if not is_admin_user(current_user) and current_user.plan != "elite":` — an Elite user is never balance-checked)
server/routes_dump.py:644-647 (the CHARGE: same condition, so an Elite user is never billed)
server/routes_dump.py:647 (an unlocked read-modify-write — the same class as REL-01: `bal = settings.get(...); settings["token_balance"] = max(0.0, bal - actual_token_cost)`)
server/credits.py:311-323 (is_unmetered — correctly operator-only; the docstring explicitly says Elite is metered and that the old `plan == "elite"` short-circuit was removed for exactly this reason)
evidence.repro: grep -nE 'plan != "elite"|is_unmetered' server/routes_dump.py  -> :422 and :644. Read both; the same condition guards the gate and the debit. As an Elite user with token_balance 0, POST the dump finalize endpoint: it returns success and token_balance is unchanged.
evidence.observed: Read at HEAD. Both conditions present. The charge path at :647 also clamps with max(0.0, ...), so even where it DOES run it moves any shortfall onto the platform rather than recording an overdraft — the opposite of the documented post-hoc settlement rule.

findings.impact: Elite is the $40 tier, and dump finalization is the expensive path — it is the LLM assignment-generation work, the single most costly thing the product does. An Elite subscriber can run it without limit at zero token cost. This is the exact failure `is_unmetered`'s docstring says was fixed ('a $40 subscription could consume unbounded upstream model spend') and it survived in this file. The gate bypass is the worse of the two: it means an Elite account with an exhausted balance is never refused.

dependents: routes_dump.py:737-749 (the batch loop, which sums `tokens_charged` — so batch totals under-report for Elite)
routes_dump.py:773-774 (total_charged_tokens / total_charged_usd, used for the batch cost preview)

fix.approach: Delete both `and current_user.plan != "elite"` clauses and let `is_unmetered()` be the single authority, then route the debit through the new atomic helper so the charge is also concurrency-safe.

if not is_unmetered(current_user):

def test_elite_is_charged_for_dump_finalization():
    """Elite is a 270,000-token allowance, not unlimited spend."""
    from server.credits import get_token_balance, is_unmetered
    from server.database import SessionLocal, User

    db = SessionLocal()
    elite = User(public_id="elite-audit-1", plan="elite", credits=0.0, role="user",
                 settings={"token_balance": 5000.0})
    db.add(elite); db.commit(); db.refresh(elite)
    try:
        assert is_unmetered(elite) is False, (
            "Elite must stay METERED — only the operator is exempt")
        assert get_token_balance(elite) == 5000.0
    finally:
        db.close()

    # The gate itself: as a metered user, an insufficient balance must be refused.
    import inspect
    from server import routes_dump
    src = inspect.getsource(routes_dump)
    assert 'plan != "elite"' not in src, (
        "an Elite plan check still bypasses the token gate/charge in routes_dump")

findings.title: Dump cost ESTIMATE is inconsistent with the current token unit and OVERestimates, so the gate can refuse users who can afford the work
findings.correction: The report said the divisor causes a ~4x UNDERcharge. Traced by hand, it does the opposite: routes_dump.py:399 computes `ceil((in + out*1.5)/1000)` task tokens, i.e. it treats 1000 model tokens as one task token, and :400 then prices that at $0.01/token. Against the live unit (100 tokens = 1 cent, credits.TOKENS_PER_USD = 10_000) and a flash rate of ~$0.15/1M input tokens, 1000 model tokens really cost ~1.5 task tokens but is quoted ~1.9, and est_cost_usd is overstated by ~100x. This is an ESTIMATE used by the pre-flight gate, not the charge, which is why it is medium and not high.

evidence.repro: python3: for a 1000-token item, _calculate_dump_item_cost returns est_cost_tokens ~2 and est_cost_usd 0.02. Compare with calculate_task_token_cost(0.00015) for the same real cost -> ~2 tokens. The USD figure is ~100x the real money.
evidence.observed: Read at HEAD. The function never calls calculate_task_token_cost and re-derives the conversion by hand with a different divisor, so it cannot track the unit.

findings.impact: The gate compares a user's real balance against an inflated estimate, so a user with enough tokens can be told 'insufficient tokens' and refused. It also reports a dollar figure that is wrong by two orders of magnitude wherever it is surfaced to the user or the operator.

fix.approach: Delete the hand-rolled conversion and use the canonical one, so the estimate tracks the unit automatically. Keep the estimate coarse — it is a gate, not a bill — but make it a consistent order of magnitude.

snippets.anchor:
est_cost_tokens = max(1, int(math.ceil((est_input_tokens + est_output_tokens * 1.5) / 1000.0)))
    est_cost_usd = round(est_cost_tokens * 0.01, 2)
snippets.before:
est_cost_tokens = max(1, int(math.ceil((est_input_tokens + est_output_tokens * 1.5) / 1000.0)))
    est_cost_usd = round(est_cost_tokens * 0.01, 2)
snippets.after:
# Price the estimated model tokens at the model's real rate and convert with the
    # CANONICAL helper, so this cannot drift from the token unit again. The previous
    # hand-rolled `/ 1000` + `* 0.01` predated the 100-tokens-per-cent change and
    # overstated the dollar cost by ~100x while over-quoting the token cost, which made
    # the gate refuse users who could afford the work.
    from .credits import calculate_task_token_cost
    _in_rate, _out_rate = _rate_for_estimate()
    est_cost_usd = (est_input_tokens / 1_000_000.0) * _in_rate + (est_output_tokens / 1_000_000.0) * _out_rate
    est_cost_tokens = max(1, calculate_task_token_cost(est_cost_usd))

fix.migration: _rate_for_estimate() should read MODEL_RATES for the model this path will actually use (deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash) rather than hardcoding a rate. If that is inconvenient, pass the rate in — but do NOT hardcode a second copy of the conversion.
fix.risk: A lower estimate means less headroom in the gate, so a user near the limit may now be allowed through and then charged more than the estimate. That is acceptable because the charge is measured post-hoc (allow_negative), but the UI copy should say the estimate is an estimate.

tests.name: test_estimate_tracks_the_canonical_token_unit
tests.proves: the estimate uses calculate_task_token_cost and is within an order of magnitude of the real cost
tests.body:
def test_estimate_tracks_the_canonical_token_unit():
    from server.routes_dump import _calculate_dump_item_cost
    from server.credits import calculate_task_token_cost

    class _Item:
        extracted_text = "x" * 4000   # ~1000 model input tokens

    est_in, est_out, est_tokens, est_usd = _calculate_dump_item_cost(_Item())

    # Flash is ~$0.15/1M in, ~$0.60/1M out. 1000 in + 600 out is ~$0.0005.
    assert est_usd < 0.01, (
        f"estimate says ${est_usd} for work that costs well under a cent")
    # And the token figure must agree with the canonical conversion of its own USD figure.
    assert est_tokens == max(1, calculate_task_token_cost(est_usd)), (
        "the estimate does not round-trip through the canonical conversion")

findings.title: REFUTED — vision calls are NOT unmetered; the metering context is bound on every authenticated path
findings.original_claim: 'Screen vision LLM calls bypass metering entirely — watermark retrieval skips meter_user(), so the user context is absent and the cost recorder returns early.'
findings.correction: The recorder does read the context (screen_vision.py:388-391 calls current_meter_user()), and that context IS populated: set_meter_user() is called from server/security.py:481-483 inside the auth binding every authenticated request funnels through, and again from api_keys.py:275-276 for key auth. The vision path therefore has a user in context and its cost is recorded. This matches the architecture note in AGENTS.md: the binding lives in the auth path so every endpoint is covered automatically, 'rather than the endpoints someone remembered to touch'.
findings.verified_by: grep -rn "meter_user" server/*.py -> setter called at security.py:481, api_keys.py:275, orchestrator.py:133,306. Reader at screen_vision.py:388. The claim that nothing sets it is false.
findings.residual_risk: Real and narrow: a background THREAD (not an asyncio task) does not inherit the contextvar, so a vision call made from a thread pool would drop its cost as unattributed. The agent paths self-set (orchestrator.py:133,306) so this is not currently live. Worth a regression test asserting the context is populated on the vision path, not a fix.

durable_notes.evidence: Compiled `db.query(User).filter(...).with_for_update()` and read the emitted SQL: it contains no `FOR UPDATE`. SQLite has no row locks to take, so the call is silently inert.
durable_notes.consequence: ANY finding whose proposed fix is 'add with_for_update()' is INERT on this database. It looks like a fix, passes review, and protects nothing. Two mechanisms actually work: `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` (serialises a read-modify-write) and expressing the change inside a single statement via json_set/json_extract (atomic with no lock).
durable_notes.found_by: Discovered while implementing REL-01 — the first version of that fix used with_for_update and would have shipped as dead code. Caught by compiling the statement rather than trusting the API name.

durable_notes.note: A read-then-write on the settings JSON blob cannot be fixed by locking ADVICE — the change must go inside the statement.
durable_notes.evidence: Measured: two concurrent 400-token debits against a 1000-token balance left 600 (one debit swallowed, both callers told they succeeded). Neither BEGIN IMMEDIATE nor with_for_update helped, because the caller computed the new balance in Python from a value read before the other committed.
durable_notes.consequence: Use credits.debit_tokens_atomic for any token delta. It applies the change in the database. There is no lock-based alternative for a value the caller derives.
durable_notes.found_by: test_concurrent_token_charges_do_not_overdraw — a sequential test passes against the broken code, so concurrency findings need threads released by a Barrier.

durable_notes.note: `plan == "elite"` bypasses are a RECURRING class in this repo, not a one-off.
durable_notes.evidence: credits.is_unmetered()'s own docstring records that this was fixed once ('a $40 subscription could consume unbounded upstream model spend'), yet routes_dump.py:422 and :644 both still carry it.
durable_notes.consequence: Grep for `plan != "elite"` / `plan == "elite"` as a routine check, not just when a finding names it. is_unmetered() is the single authority and it is operator-only. A tier check in a money path is a bug on sight.
durable_notes.found_by: Verifying agy's ECON-04, which over-claimed '~12 routes' — there was exactly one site, but it bypassed the gate AND the charge.

durable_notes.note: The test DB is a persistent FILE, so row-count assertions against a literal are flakes.
durable_notes.evidence: Two documented pre-existing reds are caused by this (test_study_tools_v3, test_browser_search_with_math_query).
durable_notes.consequence: Use a unique public_id (uuid) per test. Never assert an exact global row count.

durable_notes.note: THE TOKEN ALLOWANCES ARE A PRICED MARGIN MODEL — do not 'rebalance' them.
durable_notes.evidence: Owner ruling 2026-09-22 with arithmetic checked: 1 token = 1/100 cent = $0.0001. basic $10 -> 30,000 tok = $3.00 max service = 70.0% margin (3.33x); pro $20 -> 100,000 = $10.00 = 50.0% (2.00x); elite $40 -> 270,000 = $27.00 = 32.5% (1.48x). Trial 15,000 and testing 10,000 are grants.
durable_notes.consequence: The BALANCE is the ceiling that enforces the margin. Any code path that lets a plan spend without decrementing its balance destroys the guarantee — that is ECON-04. Never add a plan-based charge exemption; `is_unmetered()` is operator-only and must stay that way. If a future change needs different margins, change the ALLOWANCE numbers, never the gating.

decisions.question: Does fixing ECON-04 change what an Elite subscription includes?
decisions.ruling: NO CHANGE TO THE TIERS. basic = 30,000 / pro = 100,000 / elite = 270,000 reserved exactly as they are. Owner's intent stated verbatim: the allowances exist so there is a 'mathematically ensured profit margin per tier', because each token is 1/100 of a cent.
decisions.consequence: ECON-04's fix is REQUIRED, not optional — it is what enforces the owner's margin model. Elite's exemption is the only thing standing between the design and the guarantee.

arithmetic_verified.mechanism: The BALANCE is the ceiling. Every task deducts measured cost; at zero the gate refuses; so maximum lifetime service cost is allowance x $0.0001. An unlimited spend path removes the ceiling and with it the arithmetic guarantee.

decisions.note: An Elite subscriber at zero tokens will start being refused, exactly as Basic and Pro already are. That is the intended behaviour, not a regression.

decisions.question: Are task tokens refundable?
decisions.ruling: Only refunding is EARN-ONLY. Tokens are consumed, not refunded.
decisions.consequence: No refund path is added for consumed tokens. A task that fails OUTRIGHT is simply never charged (nothing is charged before work runs), which is a different mechanism and stays.
decisions.note: This is consistent with the failure semantics already in the code: allow_negative settlement after work, no up-front charge.
